evals.prompt: We have a RAG assistant that answers HR policy questions for Acme's 3,000 employees from a 400-page handbook. We're about to swap the model and rewrite the system prompt. We have about 1,200 real logged questions from the last quarter, and HR has hand-labeled 80 of them with correct answers. The answer that hurts most is confidently wrong parental-leave or termination guidance. Design the eval harness so we don't ship a regression.
assertions: The golden set is split into representative, adversarial/edge, and regression buckets, with a case count and sourcing stated for each
Representative cases are drawn from the 1,200 logged questions and 80 HR labels the user supplied; any synthetic or model-generated cases are flagged as weak evidence
Each bucket or case names its grading method, and programmatic or structured-assertion checks are preferred over LLM-as-judge where the output is checkable
If an LLM judge is used (e.g. for faithfulness), it has its own rubric, is validated against the HR human labels, and controls for position, verbosity, and self-preference bias
The metric, the no-regression gate against baseline, and a critical subset (parental-leave and termination answers) held at 100% are all set before any run
A held-out split is defined and the rule against tuning on the test set is stated explicitly
Cost per run and p95 latency are tracked alongside the quality metric
A failure taxonomy (e.g. hallucination, refusal, missed-edge-case) is defined so iteration targets the biggest bucket

evals.prompt: I'm the ML engineer on the 'Ask a Pharmacist' assistant at Tollgate Pharmacy (a chain of 85 pharmacies). It's a chatbot on our website that answers questions about over-the-counter medicines using our patient information leaflets. The details are in `feature-brief.md`, what we test today is in `current-tests.md`, incidents are in `incident-log.md`, and the PM's request and our data situation are in `pm-request.md`. Design the evaluation we should put in place before the next prompt change ships. Two pages max.
assertions: It points out that 14 of 15 passing is not a 100% pass rate, and that 15 developer-written questions about adult use do not test the rules or the incidents
It turns each of the three logged incidents (the child's Calmexa dose, the discontinued Nasaclear, the invented Dormilene and Ferrovit interaction) into test cases that must be in the test set
It does not rely on an average judge score alone: a failure on the under-12 dosing rule (and similar safety rules) blocks release on its own, whatever the average

It does not rely on an unchecked LLM judge: it checks some rules directly (such as the 120-word limit or whether the pharmacist referral is offered), or checks the judge against pharmacists' grading, or both
It does not use the 9,400 chat-log questions until redaction is approved, and says what to use in the meantime
It does not invent incidents, products or figures that are not in the files
It is no longer than two pages

evals.prompt: I'm a secondary school English teacher. I made a custom GPT that marks students' essays out of 20 and writes feedback. Before I use it for report grades I want to know it marks fairly. I've got last year's 40 essays that I marked myself. How do I test it? A few bullets please.
assertions: It uses her 40 marked essays as the answer key: run the GPT on them and compare its marks with hers
It says to decide in advance how close counts as good enough (for example within a stated number of marks on most essays) rather than eyeballing the results
It checks for specific kinds of unfairness, such as marks rising with essay length or doing worse on particular types of essay or student, not only the overall average
It says to retest on the same essays whenever she changes the GPT's instructions
It keeps the teacher in charge of the final report grades, for example by checking the GPT's marks before they count
It does not invent results or statistics about her essays
It is a few bullets in plain language
